extraction.name: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects)
extraction.description: A word-prediction benchmark consisting of 10,022 narrative passages whose final word can be predicted by humans from the whole passage but not from the final sentence alone. It contains 4,869 development passages and 5,153 test passages, with a separate training corpus of 2,662 novels comprising 203 million words.
extraction.creator: Denis Papemo, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bemardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Femández
extraction.citeAs: The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031v1 [cs.CL], 20 June 2016.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Narrative passages were extracted from the Book Corpus after duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material. Novels were randomly divided into training and development/testing partitions, with development and test novels also kept disjoint. Each passage contains a target sentence and the minimum number of preceding complete sentences needed to provide at least 50 context tokens. Passages relatively easy for any of four language models were excluded. A random sample of the remaining passages underwent three-stage human filtering through CrowdFlower: two successive subjects had to predict the final word correctly using the whole passage, while subjects given only the target sentence had to fail to predict it.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), containing unpublished novels. After duplicate removal and filtering potentially offensive material using a stop word list, the source corpus contained 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The final word of each target sentence was withheld for the prediction task, with the original word retained as the correct answer. Novels were randomly partitioned so that training, development, and test data came from disjoint novels.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicates were removed and potentially offensive material was filtered using a stop word list. Contexts were constructed from complete sentences cumulatively containing at least 50 tokens before the target sentence. Automated filtering used a pretrained RNN and three models trained on the Book Corpus: a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model. A passage was excluded if any model assigned its target word probability greater than or equal to 0.00175. Human filtering then retained only passages predictable from broad context but not from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: CrowdFlower subjects guessed the original final word of a target sentence. First, one subject saw the whole passage; only a correct response advanced the item. Second, another subject saw the whole passage; another correct response was required. Third, subjects saw only the target sentence, with up to three guesses per sentence, until the word was guessed or the unsuccessful-guess threshold was reached. Only items passing all stages were retained. A subject could not judge the same item in both whole-passage and sentence-only conditions. Subjects were paid $0.22 per page of 10 passages in the first two stages and $0.15 per page of 20 sentences in the third stage.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Selection used strict exact matching to the original missing word rather than accepting synonyms or other plausible continuations. Two consecutive correct whole-passage predictions were required because a pilot study showed that a single correct prediction could reflect an especially able or lucky subject. Sentence-only testing excluded locally predictable items. Evaluating alternative acceptable answers with additional raters was considered financially and practically infeasible. Approximately 84–86% of items were discarded at stage 1, another 6–7% at stage 2, and another 3–5% at stage 3; approximately one in 25 input examples survived.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For retained passages, two subjects correctly predicted the word from the whole passage. The paper also states that none of ten sentence-only subjects could predict it, even with three guesses each.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus were available for download from the dataset website. The authors planned a public competition and stated that the test set would be made available at the time of that competition. No updating schedule, versioning policy, or deprecation policy is specified.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: More than 80% of passages contain the target word in the context, compared with less than 15% of input passages; approximately 84% contain its lemma. Proper nouns are overrepresented at 48% of targets, followed by common nouns at 37% and verbs at 7.7%; pronouns account for only 0.3%. All proper-noun targets were confirmed to occur in the context. Sentence-final positioning favors nouns, and human filtering further favors nouns over other parts of speech. Quoted direct speech occurs in 71% of LAMBADA items versus 61% of input items. Automated selection deliberately favors passages on which the filtering language models fail.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Strict exact-match selection excludes passages where humans provide plausible alternatives or synonyms rather than the original word. Cost considerations prevented using more subjects at the first filtering stage. The task appears to favor co-reference over some event-related discourse phenomena. Lemmatization errors affected analysis of fictional proper names. Standard language models are disadvantaged by design because automated filtering removed passages they could predict. The training corpus is from the same domain but is not filtered in the same way as the development and test passages.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluating general-purpose language models on broad-context understanding through final-word prediction. The separate raw-text training corpus supports ordinary language-model training, and the development set can be used for hyperparameter tuning and fine-tuning to passage characteristics. The authors recommend training models on predicting upcoming words from preceding context in unsupervised text, rather than developing ad-hoc models exclusively for the final-word task. They emphasize that models should handle ordinary language-modeling cases as well as the harder LAMBADA cases.
